title: "Applying Deep Learning to Earth Observation"

## Overview 

Focusing on convolutional and recurrent neural networks, *Applying Deep Learning to Earth Observation* is designed to provide a hands-on introduction to deep learning algorithms and their application to satellite imagery, with a fairly strong emphasis on the task of semantic segmentation (or image classification). The course is designed to provide students with:

- A basic knowledge of the classes of neural networks useful for analyzing EO data;
- The key components of neural networks, particularly convolutional neural networks; 
- The skills needed to undertake a complete image classification workflow, including how to acquire and process imagery into the necesssary formats, how to develop and train a model, and how to make and critically evaluate the resulting maps. 

The course is both theoretical and hands-on. The hands-pn component emphasizes the use of programming (python), including AI-assisted coding, the use of open image archives and EO analytical platforms (e.g. Google Earth Engine), and tools for creating open and reproducible workflows (git and GitHub). The theoretical component emphasizes an understanding the variety and components of neural network architectures, training and evaluation approaches, and other important considerations.   

## Materials

The course material is developed from a wide variety of openly available resources, but draws in particular from a [comprehensive synthesis paper](http://arxiv.org/abs/2308.09221) led by Sam Khallaghi (currently in revision). Another important resource is [Dive into Deep Learning](https://d2l.ai/index.html). References to other sources are provided throughout the course unit documents. The details about readings, assignments, and projects are found in the course [syllabus](syllabus.qmd). 

## Projects

In addition to readings and assignments, students will work on a final project, for which they will work together in small teams to apply deep learning to solve problems related to ongoing research projects, such as a cropland mapping project (see @fig-1).
